meta.title: Who really said "What is important is seldom urgent and what is urgent is seldom important"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Eisenhower said it in 1954 — but not in these words, and he credited an unnamed former college president. The “seldom” version is a listener's paraphrase.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'What is important is seldom urgent and what is urgent is seldom important'?
meta.ogDescription: At Evanston in 1954 he quoted an unnamed college president: “the important are never urgent.” The hedged “seldom” wording came later, from listeners.

answer.label: Not Eisenhower’s wording — and he was quoting someone else
answer.authorName: An unnamed “former college president” — quoted by Dwight D. Eisenhower
answer.authorDates: Quoted by Dwight D. Eisenhower (1890–1969) at Evanston, Illinois, 19 August 1954
answer.sourceLine: Eisenhower did put this idea into a speech — his address to the Second Assembly of the World Council of Churches at Evanston, Illinois, on 19 August 1954 — but his words were absolute, not hedged: “I have two kinds of problems, the urgent and the important. The urgent are not important, and the important are never urgent.” The word “seldom” appears nowhere in the speech. And he prefaced the line by saying he was “quoting the statement of a former college president,” a man neither Eisenhower nor any later researcher has identified. The familiar “seldom…seldom” version most likely began as a listener’s paraphrase that hardened into a quotation; Quote Investigator also allows that Eisenhower may have used more than one version of the expression, though no second version has ever been produced.
answer.confidenceText: Disputed — the thought is real and the 1954 speech is documented, but the popular wording is a retelling, and Eisenhower explicitly declined the credit.

source.heading: What Eisenhower actually said

docMeta.dd: Address at the Second Assembly of the World Council of Churches, Evanston, Illinois
19 August 1954, on the campus of Northwestern University, Evanston, Illinois
“The urgent are not important, and the important are never urgent” — no “seldom” anywhere in the speech
A listener’s recollection printed in the Life Office Management Association annual conference proceedings, 1954, p. 16 (per Quote Investigator)

source.excerpt: Now, my friends of this convocation, there is another thing we can hope to learn from your being with us. I illustrate it by quoting the statement of a former college president, and I can understand the reason for his speaking as he did. I am sure President Miller can. This President said, ‘I have two kinds of problems, the urgent and the important. The urgent are not important, and the important are never urgent.’
trail: 19 August 1954 — addressing the Second Assembly of the World Council of Churches at Evanston, Eisenhower says he will “illustrate it by quoting the statement of a former college president,” who had said: “I have two kinds of problems, the urgent and the important. The urgent are not important, and the important are never urgent.” The word “seldom” is not in the speech (American Presidency Project ↗).

Later in 1954 — the earliest “seldom” wording in Quote Investigator’s chronology. A speaker at a Life Office Management Association conference, Morris G. Fuller of State Farm Life Insurance, relays the recollection of Norris Pitt, who had heard the Evanston address: “the things that are urgent are seldom important and the things that are important are seldom urgent” — QI cites Fuller’s talk in the conference proceedings, start page 12, quote page 16 (Quote Investigator ↗).

1962 — the phrase turns up in fiction. John le Carré’s A Murder of Quality has a character say “what is important is seldom urgent. Urgent equals ephemeral, and ephemeral equals unimportant” — QI cites page 111 of the 1980 Bantam Books edition of the novel first published in 1962 (Quote Investigator ↗).

1973 and 1975 — newspapers attach the softened version to Eisenhower without quotation marks: the Winnipeg Free Press (“the really important matters were seldom urgent, and that the most urgent matters were seldom important”) and the Christian Science Monitor (“important matters were seldom urgent and most urgent matters were seldom important”) (Quote Investigator ↗).
source.excerptNote: The passage in full, from the official transcript. Two details do all the work: Eisenhower attributes the maxim to a former college president — while addressing Northwestern’s sitting president, J. Roscoe Miller, as a separate person in the very next clause — and his phrasing is absolute (“never urgent”), not hedged.

sourceLink.text: Quote Investigator: the full citation history

source.rightsNote: No rights status can honestly be asserted for the line as it circulates. Eisenhower’s 19 August 1954 address is a work of the United States government and carries no copyright — but the popular “seldom…seldom” sentence is not in it. That wording traces to listeners’ paraphrases whose author and first fixed publication cannot be pinned down, and the printed appearances Quote Investigator documents (1954 conference proceedings, a 1962 novel, 1970s newspapers) are all post-1930 texts belonging to their publishers — none of which is a source for an Eisenhower utterance, only a repetition of one.

author.name: Dwight D. Eisenhower
author.kicker: The man who gets the credit
author.heading: The general who passed the line along
author.metaLine: 1890–1969 · Supreme Commander, Allied Expeditionary Force · 34th President of the United States
author.bio: Eisenhower commanded the Allied Expeditionary Force in Europe from 1943 to 1945 and served as the 34th President of the United States from 1953 to 1961. A reputation for ruthless prioritisation is exactly why a maxim about sorting the urgent from the important stuck to his name so readily — the productivity world still calls the resulting grid the Eisenhower Method. But at Evanston he was passing along someone else’s observation and said so plainly: the “former college president” he credited has never been identified.

copyAttribution: Dwight D. Eisenhower did not say "What is important is seldom urgent and what is urgent is seldom important." Addressing the Second Assembly of the World Council of Churches at Evanston, Illinois, on 19 August 1954, he quoted "the statement of a former college president": "I have two kinds of problems, the urgent and the important. The urgent are not important, and the important are never urgent." The word "seldom" does not appear in the speech, and Eisenhower did not claim the line as his own. Quote Investigator traces the hedged wording to listeners' retellings beginning later in 1954. — Quotle.info

misattribution.heading: A double misattribution
misattribution.intro: Two separate things are wrong here, and a third “correction” that circulates online is wrong too. The wording isn’t Eisenhower’s; the thought isn’t Eisenhower’s; and the man usually named as the real source isn’t the real source either.

items.why: What he said at Evanston was absolute: “The urgent are not important, and the important are never urgent.” Not “seldom” — never. The hedged version appears nowhere in the transcript (American Presidency Project ↗).

He introduced the line with “I illustrate it by quoting the statement of a former college president” — an explicit refusal of the credit. Quote Investigator concludes he “credited an unnamed ‘former college president’” and does not identify the man (Quote Investigator ↗).

items.who: J. Roscoe Miller, president of Northwestern University
items.why: A popular “correction” names Miller as the college president Eisenhower was quoting — Wikipedia’s Priority Matrix ↗ article still says the remark “was delivered as a quote from sitting president of Northwestern University J. Roscoe Miller.” But Eisenhower said former president, and referred to Miller separately in the same breath (“I am sure President Miller can”). Quote Investigator is blunt about it: “Eisenhower was not ascribing the saying to Miller who was a current president and not a former president” (Quote Investigator ↗).

misattribution.truthLine: The documented fact is a modest one: on 19 August 1954 Eisenhower repeated, in absolute terms, a maxim he attributed to an unnamed former college president — and the hedged “seldom” version that now carries his name grew out of listeners’ retellings, beginning later that same year (Quote Investigator ↗).

context.heading: Why the paraphrase beat the original
lead: The line Eisenhower actually repeated is a harder, funnier claim than the one that now circulates. “The urgent are not important, and the important are never urgent” is an absolute — a paradox stated with no escape hatch, which is what makes it land in a speech. The version that survived softens both halves to “seldom,” converting an aphorism into something closer to a defensible management rule. That is almost certainly why it spread: it is the form you can actually build a matrix on.

And build one people did. The urgent/important grid is known as the Eisenhower Method ↗, and Wikipedia’s own account of it prints the 1954 sentence while noting that “Eisenhower did not claim this insight for his own, but attributed it to an unnamed ‘former college president.’” The framework carries a name its namesake never asked for, built on a sentence he never quite said.
context.detailsSummary: How a 1954 speech turned into a quotation
detailsBody: Quote Investigator’s chronology shows the drift happening almost immediately. Later in 1954, a speaker at a Life Office Management Association conference passed on the recollection of an attendee at the Evanston address, in the softened form — QI cites the conference proceedings at page 16. By 1962 the phrase “what is important is seldom urgent” had migrated into fiction, in John le Carré’s A Murder of Quality. By the 1970s newspapers were attaching the softened version straight to Eisenhower.

QI leaves one door open, and so do we: it notes that as an alternative to faulty transmission, “Eisenhower may have used more than one version of the expression.” No such second version has been produced. Until one is, the transcript of 19 August 1954 is the only documented thing Eisenhower said on the subject — and it does not contain the sentence people quote.
